rationales.C: Standard III(A) Compliance Practices states: 'Diversify: Members and candidates should diversify investments to reduce the risk of loss, unless diversification is not consistent with plan guidelines or is contrary to the account objectives.' Diversification to reduce the risk of loss is therefore the general practice, subject to those two exceptions: the plan's own guidelines, and the objectives of the particular account.

questions.stem: A broker offers Carter new execution-only trades at low fees comparable to those of the brokers Carter currently uses, and commissions on the new service count toward the firm's soft dollar commitment. Carter's most appropriate course of action is to:

options.A: increase trading volume to meet the soft dollar commitment.
options.B: use the new service for accounts that prohibit soft dollar arrangements.
options.C: avoid the new service for all accounts.

rationales.A: Carter should not artificially increase trading volume. Generating trades in order to accumulate commissions toward a soft dollar commitment serves the firm's arrangement rather than the client, places the clients' interests behind the manager's, and costs the accounts commissions they would not otherwise have paid.
rationales.B: Carter can trade for his accounts that prohibit soft dollar arrangements under the new, low-fee trading scheme. The new trades are execution-only and priced comparably to the fees other brokers currently used charge, so they do not carry the elevated commission that is what a soft dollar arrangement actually costs a client. The prohibition in those accounts is aimed at the client paying a surcharge above competitive rates to fund goods or services; it is not violated when trades are executed at competitive market rates, even though the firm's own commission tally benefits.
rationales.C: Declining the service for every account is more restrictive than the duty requires. Execution-only trades at fees comparable to those of the brokers already in use involve no soft-dollar surcharge borne by the client, so they are available even for accounts whose terms prohibit soft dollar arrangements.

questions.stem: A manager's use of client brokerage commissions most likely violates Standard III(A) when the commissions pay for:

options.A: services that benefit the client commensurately.
options.B: services the client has directed the manager to obtain.
options.C: the investment manager's operating expenses.

rationales.A: This is the proper use. Client brokerage is an asset of the client, so commissions should be spent on goods or services that benefit the client, and the benefit received should be commensurate with the commission paid. Standard III(A) guidance on soft commission policies states that a member or candidate who pays a higher brokerage commission than he or she would normally pay to allow for the purchase of goods or services, without corresponding benefit to the client, violates the duty of loyalty to the client. Where the benefit does correspond, the duty is met.
rationales.B: Directed brokerage is permitted. A client may direct the manager to use a specific brokerage firm, and because the commission is the client's asset used for that client's benefit, the practice does not itself violate the duty of loyalty. The member should seek confirmation that the goods or services purchased will benefit the account beneficiaries and should disclose that the client may not be getting best execution, but the arrangement is not a violation.
rationales.C: Client brokerage commissions may not be directed to pay the investment manager's operating expenses. This violates the duty of loyalty because brokerage commissions are an asset of the client, not of the manager; spending them on the manager's own overhead means client assets are funding costs the manager or the manager's employer should bear, and the benefit runs to the manager rather than to the client. Standard III(A) guidance on soft commission policies states: 'A member or candidate who pays a higher brokerage commission than he or she would normally pay to allow for the purchase of goods or services, without corresponding benefit to the client, violates the duty of loyalty to the client.'

questions.stem: Stafford pays her CFA Program registration and exam fees out of her fund's soft dollar account, and the fund's prospectus discloses its soft dollar policies. Stafford's use of the account is most likely:

options.A: permitted, given the prospectus disclosure.
options.B: a violation, because the benefit is personal.
options.C: a violation, because the program is not research.

rationales.A: Disclosure of soft dollar policies in the prospectus does not convert a personal benefit into a client benefit. Improving Stafford's own investment skills and credentials is a professional and career benefit to her, and the registration and exam fees are an expense she or her employer should bear rather than fund shareholders. Disclosure describes how the account is used; it does not make an otherwise improper use of client commissions proper.
rationales.B: Stafford violated the Code and Standards because improving her investment skills is not a reasonable use of the soft dollar account. Soft dollars may buy research services that benefit the client, but personal certification fees benefit Stafford personally and represent an expense that should be borne by her or her employer, not by fund shareholders. Even with the prospectus disclosing the fund's soft-dollar policies, using client commissions for personal development is a breach of the duty of loyalty, because the commissions are an asset of the client and must be spent for the client's benefit.
rationales.C: Whether the CFA Program meets a definition of research is not the determining issue. The violation lies in the direction of the benefit: client commissions were used to pay for a personal credential, an expense that belongs to Stafford or her employer. Framing the problem as a classification question misses that even a plausibly research-like expenditure must benefit the client to be a permissible use of soft dollars.

questions.stem: Under Standard III(A), a member whose client directs that trades be placed with a specific brokerage firm is most likely expected to:

options.A: decline the arrangement as a best-execution violation.
options.B: accept the direction without further disclosure.
options.C: disclose that the client may not receive best execution.

rationales.A: Directed brokerage is permissible, not an inherent violation. Because the brokerage commission is an asset of the client and is used to benefit that client rather than the manager, the practice does not violate the duty of loyalty. What the duty requires is not refusal but disclosure of the potential consequence for execution quality, together with confirmation from the client that what is purchased from the brokerage will benefit the account beneficiaries.
rationales.B: Accepting the direction is permitted, but silence is not. Precisely because the commissions are the client's own asset, the member should seek confirmation from the client that the goods or services purchased from the brokerage will benefit the account beneficiaries, and should disclose to the client that the client may not be getting best execution from the directed brokerage. The client's having chosen the broker is the reason for the disclosure, not a reason to omit it.
rationales.C: When clients direct the manager to use a specific brokerage firm for trades, the brokerage commission is an asset of the client and is used to benefit that client, not the manager, so the practice does not violate the duty of loyalty. The member or candidate should, however, seek confirmation from the client that the goods or services purchased from the brokerage will benefit the account beneficiaries, and should disclose to the client that the client may not be getting best execution from the directed brokerage. Standard III(A) guidance on soft commission policies states: 'From time to time, some clients will direct a manager to use a specific brokerage firm for all or some of the client's trades... The member or candidate should, however, seek confirmation from the client that the goods or services purchased from the brokerage will benefit the account beneficiaries. In addition, the member or candidate should disclose to the client that the client may not be getting best execution from the directed brokerage.'

questions.stem: Under Standard III(B), an initial investment recommendation is most appropriately made available to:

options.A: the clients with the largest accounts first.
options.B: all clients, whatever their interest or its suitability.
options.C: all clients who indicate an interest.

rationales.A: This bases dissemination on preferred or favored status. The selection process by which customers receive information should rest on suitability and known interest, not on account size, relationship value, or any other favored standing. Giving the largest accounts first access is the fair-dealing failure the practice is written to prevent.
rationales.B: This mandates over-broad dissemination. A member or candidate need not communicate a recommendation to all customers; the practice is to make initial recommendations available to clients based on suitability and indicated interest. Pushing every recommendation to every client regardless of suitability misstates the duty, which is about the fairness of the selection process rather than universal distribution.
rationales.C: The practice is to make initial investment recommendations available to all clients who indicate an interest. Although a member or candidate need not communicate a recommendation to all customers, the selection process by which customers receive information should be based on suitability and known interest, not on any preferred or favored status, and a common practice to ensure fair dealing is to communicate recommendations simultaneously within the firm and to customers. Standard III(B) Compliance Practices states: 'Disseminate investment recommendations based on indications of interest and suitability: Make initial investment recommendations available to all clients who indicate an interest. Although a member or candidate need not communicate a recommendation to all customers, the selection process by which customers receive information should be based on suitability and known interest, not on any preferred or favored status. A common practice to ensure fair dealing is to communicate recommendations simultaneously within the firm and to customers.'

questions.stem: Under Standard III(B), awareness that an investment recommendation is about to be disseminated is most appropriately extended to:

options.A: everyone on the trading floor.
options.B: as few people as reasonably possible.
options.C: anyone who signs a confidentiality notice.

rationales.A: The practice runs the other way: limit the number of people who are aware that a recommendation is going to be disseminated. Alerting the trading floor so that execution can be staged widens the circle of people who could act ahead of clients, which is the risk the practice is written to contain.
rationales.B: Standard III(B) Compliance Practices states: 'Limit the number of people involved: Members and candidates should make reasonable efforts to limit the number of people who are aware that a recommendation is going to be disseminated.' Keeping the circle small is the control, because every additional person with advance knowledge is another channel through which the information can be acted on before clients have had a fair opportunity.
rationales.C: A signed confidentiality notice does not substitute for minimizing awareness. The practice is to make reasonable efforts to limit how many people know a recommendation is coming; the smaller the circle, the lower the front-running risk, regardless of what each person has undertaken in writing.

questions.stem: Under Standard III(B), a member with prior knowledge of a pending investment recommendation is most likely expected to:

options.A: refrain from discussing or acting on it before dissemination.
options.B: discuss it within his or her social circle.
options.C: trade on it for client accounts before its release.

rationales.A: Standard III(B) Compliance Practices states: 'Publish guidelines for predissemination behavior: Members and candidates who have prior knowledge of an investment recommendation should refrain from discussing or taking any action on the pending recommendation and must follow any firm policies regarding conduct prior to dissemination of investment recommendations.' Both halves matter: no discussion and no action on the pending recommendation, and compliance with whatever predissemination policies the firm has adopted.
rationales.B: Discussing the pending recommendation is exactly what predissemination guidance restricts, and the setting makes no difference. Those with prior knowledge should refrain from discussing or taking any action on the pending recommendation; a social conversation spreads the information to people who may act on it before clients have had a fair opportunity.
rationales.C: Those with prior knowledge should refrain from taking any action on the pending recommendation until clients have had a fair opportunity to act on it. Trading ahead of the release favors the accounts traded first, breaches the fair-dealing duty owed to the rest, and is action on the recommendation of the kind the firm's predissemination policies prohibit.

questions.stem: Under Standard III(B), fair dealing in the dissemination of a new investment recommendation is most likely achieved by informing:

options.A: all clients at approximately the same time.
options.B: all clients eventually, in any order.
options.C: the largest fee-paying clients first.

rationales.A: Members and candidates should establish procedures for the timing of dissemination of investment recommendations so that all clients are treated fairly, that is, informed at approximately the same time. If a firm is going to announce a new recommendation, supervisory personnel should time the announcement to avoid placing any client or group of clients at an unfair advantage relative to other clients. Once that distribution has occurred, the member or candidate may follow up separately with individual clients, but must not give favored clients advance information when such advance notification may disadvantage other clients.
rationales.B: Timing is the substance of the requirement, not an incidental detail. The procedures exist to get the information to all clients contemporaneously, so a sequence of releases that eventually reaches everyone still breaches the standard if some clients learn first and can trade on the recommendation ahead of the rest.
rationales.C: Fair treatment means that no favored tier receives the recommendation in advance. A client's fee level or economic importance to the firm creates no priority in dissemination; supervisory personnel must time the announcement so that no client or group of clients is placed at an unfair advantage relative to other clients.

questions.stem: The guiding principles that a firm's trade allocation procedures should ensure under Standard III(B) are best described as:

options.A: aggregate commission maximization.
options.B: fairness, timeliness, and record accuracy.
options.C: execution priority alone.

rationales.A: The guiding principles center on fairness to advisory clients, both in the priority of execution of orders and in the allocation of the price obtained in the execution of block orders or trades, not on firm revenue. Commission generation is not one of the principles; where commissions arise, all client accounts participating in a block trade should be charged the same commission.
rationales.B: When formulating procedures for allocating trades, members and candidates should develop a set of guiding principles that ensure, first, fairness to advisory clients, both in the priority of execution of orders and in the allocation of the price obtained in the execution of block orders or trades; second, timeliness and efficiency in the execution of orders; and third, accuracy of the member's or candidate's records as to trade orders and client account positions.
rationales.C: Execution priority is only the first of the principles. Timeliness and efficiency in the execution of orders, and accuracy of the member's or candidate's records as to trade orders and client account positions, are equally part of the set, so procedures confined to execution priority are incomplete.

questions.stem: A block trading practice that is consistent with Standard III(B) is most likely:

options.A: allocating partial fills to the largest accounts first.
options.B: time-stamping all orders, modifications, and cancellations.
options.C: pricing each account by the sequence of its fills.

rationales.A: When the full amount of a block order is not received, partially executed orders should be allocated among the participating client accounts pro rata on the basis of order size, while not going below an established minimum lot size for some securities such as bonds. Allocating by account size instead gives priority to the largest accounts and is not fair dealing.
rationales.B: Practices to consider include requiring orders and modifications or cancellations of orders to be documented and time stamped; processing and executing orders on a first-in, first-out basis, with consideration of bundling orders for efficiency as appropriate for the asset class or security; developing a policy to address such issues as calculating execution prices and partial fills when trades are grouped, or in a block, for efficiency; giving all client accounts participating in a block trade the same execution price and charging the same commission; when the full amount of the block order is not received, allocating partially executed orders among the participating client accounts pro rata on the basis of order size while not going below an established minimum lot size for some securities; and, when allocating trades for new issues, obtaining advance indications of interest, allocating securities by client rather than by portfolio manager, and providing a method for calculating allocations.
rationales.C: All client accounts participating in a block trade should be given the same execution price and charged the same commission. Assigning accounts different prices according to when their fills happened to occur gives accounts different prices within one block; the firm should instead develop a policy addressing how execution prices and partial fills are calculated when trades are grouped in a block.

questions.stem: Under Standard III(B), maintaining a list of all clients and the investments each client holds is most likely:

options.A: recommended for all clients and their holdings.
options.B: discouraged as a confidentiality hazard.
options.C: recommended only for discretionary accounts.

rationales.A: Members and candidates should maintain a list of all clients and the securities or other investments each client holds in order to facilitate notification of customers or clients of a change in an investment recommendation. If a particular security or other investment is to be sold, such a list can be used to ensure that all holders are treated fairly in the liquidation of that particular investment.
rationales.B: The list is a recommended compliance tool rather than a hazard. It is what enables the firm to notify every affected customer or client when a recommendation changes or a position is to be liquidated, and so is the mechanism by which all holders of an investment are treated fairly.
rationales.C: Fair dealing notification duties run to clients generally, not only to those whose accounts are discretionary, so the list should cover all clients and the securities or other investments each of them holds.

questions.stem: Under Standard III(C), the client identification section of an investment policy statement most likely covers:

options.A: liquidity needs and time horizon.
options.B: the type and nature of the client.
options.C: return objectives and risk tolerance.

rationales.A: Liquidity needs and investment time horizon are client constraints. The investment policy statement records them in its constraints section, alongside expected cash flows, investable funds, tax considerations, and regulatory and legal circumstances, rather than under client identification.
rationales.B: Client identification covers the type and nature of the client, the existence of separate beneficiaries, and the approximate portion of total client assets that the member or candidate is managing.
rationales.C: Return objectives and tolerance for risk are the elements of the client expectations section of the investment policy statement, not elements of client identification.

questions.stem: Under Standard III(C), the client expectations section of an investment policy statement most likely covers:

options.A: return objectives and risk tolerance.
options.B: tax considerations and legal circumstances.
options.C: client type and separate beneficiaries.

rationales.A: Client expectations comprise return objectives, covering income, growth in principal, and maintenance of purchasing power, and risk tolerance, covering suitability and stability of values.
rationales.B: Tax considerations and regulatory and legal circumstances are client constraints, recorded in the constraints section of the investment policy statement rather than under client expectations.
rationales.C: The type and nature of the client and the existence of separate beneficiaries belong to the client identification section of the investment policy statement, not to client expectations.

questions.stem: Under Standard III(C), the client constraints section of an investment policy statement most likely includes:

options.A: liquidity needs and expected cash flows.
options.B: return objectives and risk tolerance.
options.C: client type and separate beneficiaries.

rationales.A: Client constraints include liquidity needs; expected cash flows, meaning patterns of additions or withdrawals; investable funds, covering assets and liabilities or other commitments; time horizon; tax considerations; regulatory and legal circumstances; investor preferences, prohibitions, circumstances, and unique needs, such as a framework for incorporating ESG factors; and proxy voting responsibilities and guidance.
rationales.B: Return objectives, covering income, growth, and maintenance of purchasing power, and risk tolerance, covering suitability and stability of values, are the client expectations elements of the investment policy statement, not constraints.
rationales.C: The type and nature of the client and the existence of separate beneficiaries belong to the client identification section of the investment policy statement, not to the constraints section.

questions.stem: Under Standard III(C), an appropriate suitability test most likely requires the investment professional to assess:

options.A: the investment's impact on portfolio diversification.
options.B: the investment's expected return relative to peers alone.
options.C: the investment's risk in isolation from the portfolio.

rationales.A: Appropriate suitability test procedures require the investment professional to look beyond the return potential of the investment and include an analysis of the impact on the portfolio's diversification, a comparison of the investment risks with the client's assessed risk tolerance, and the fit of the investment with the required investment strategy.
rationales.B: Relative return potential is only the starting point. The test must look beyond return potential to the effect on the portfolio's diversification, the fit of the investment's risks with the client's assessed risk tolerance, and its consistency with the required investment strategy, so a test that begins and ends with expected return is not an appropriate one.
rationales.C: Risk cannot be judged in isolation. The impact on the diversification and composition of the client's existing portfolio is a core element of the suitability test, as is the comparison of the investment's risks with the client's assessed risk tolerance.

questions.stem: Under Standard III(C), regular updating of an investment policy statement most likely requires that it be:

options.A: revised only in response to market events.
options.B: revised for changes in the client's circumstances.
options.C: left unchanged once executed.

rationales.A: Changes in the client's own circumstances are a primary trigger for an update. Market conditions matter as well, since a major change in them can dictate more frequent review, but an update policy keyed only to market events would miss changed client objectives and constraints.
rationales.B: Members and candidates should periodically review the investor's objectives and constraints and reflect any changes in the client's circumstances in an updated investment policy statement. They should regularly compare client constraints with capital market expectations to arrive at an appropriate asset allocation, since changes in either factor may result in a fundamental change in asset allocation. Each client's investment policy statement should be reviewed annually unless business or other reasons, such as a major change in market conditions, dictate more frequent review.
rationales.C: Objectives and constraints must be reviewed periodically and the investment policy statement updated for changed circumstances. Wanting a stable baseline against which to judge performance does not justify leaving a stale policy statement in place, because the allocation it prescribes may no longer suit the client.

questions.stem: With respect to portions of a client's portfolio that the member does not manage, Standard III(C) most likely directs the member to:

options.A: encourage disclosure of the complete portfolio.
options.B: avoid inquiring about outside holdings.
options.C: decline to advise without full disclosure.

rationales.A: Members and candidates should encourage their clients to fully disclose their complete financial portfolio, including those portions not managed by the member or candidate, to facilitate an effective suitability determination. If clients withhold information about their financial portfolios, the suitability analysis conducted by members and candidates must be based on the information provided and cannot be expected to be complete.
rationales.B: Disclosure of the complete financial portfolio, including the portions the member does not manage, should be encouraged rather than avoided. Confining the inquiry to managed assets leaves the suitability analysis resting on a partial view of the client's holdings, which is precisely what the practice is meant to prevent.
rationales.C: The practice is encouragement, not a precondition to giving advice. Where a client withholds information about holdings elsewhere, the suitability analysis proceeds on the information provided and simply cannot be expected to be complete.

questions.stem: For a member showing the performance history of the assets she manages, compliance with the GIPS standards is most likely:

options.A: Discouraged for smaller managers as too costly.
options.B: Recommended as the best method of meeting the standard.
options.C: Legally required of anyone presenting performance.

rationales.A: Compliance with the GIPS standards is recommended as the best method of meeting Standard III(D) obligations, and that recommendation carries no carve-out for firm size. Cost and complexity are not treated as grounds for discouraging smaller managers from claiming compliance; on the contrary, members and candidates should encourage their firms to comply with the GIPS standards whatever the size of the firm.
rationales.B: For members and candidates who are showing the performance history of the assets they manage, compliance with the GIPS standards is the best method to meet their obligations under Standard III(D), and members and candidates should encourage their firms to comply with the GIPS standards. Standard III(D) requires that communication of investment performance information be fair, accurate, and complete, and the GIPS standards are the recognized framework for achieving that: they govern composite construction, the treatment of terminated accounts, required disclosures, and the retention of the data and records used to calculate the performance presented.
rationales.C: The GIPS standards are voluntary. Compliance is the recommended best method of satisfying Standard III(D) for a member or candidate showing the performance history of assets under management, but it is not a legal mandate. A member whose firm does not claim compliance can still discharge the obligation by other means, such as presenting the performance of a composite of similar portfolios rather than a single representative account, including terminated accounts, and making disclosures that fully explain the results reported.

questions.stem: A member whose firm does not comply with the GIPS standards most appropriately meets her obligations under Standard III(D) by:

options.A: tailoring the information provided to the audience's sophistication.
options.B: providing every client the same level of detail.
options.C: relying on the same boilerplate disclosure for every audience.

rationales.A: Members and candidates whose firms do not comply with the GIPS standards can meet their obligations under Standard III(D) to present a fair, accurate, and complete investment performance history by, among other things, considering the knowledge and sophistication of the audience to whom a performance presentation is addressed when determining what information to provide and tailoring it accordingly; presenting the performance of a composite of similar portfolios rather than using a single representative account; including terminated accounts as part of any composite performance history; including disclosures that fully explain the performance results being reported, for example stating when appropriate that results are simulated when model results are used, clearly indicating when the performance record is that of a prior entity, or disclosing whether the performance is gross of fees, net of fees, or after tax; and maintaining the data and records used to calculate the performance being presented.
rationales.B: Tailoring to the audience is expressly recommended, so audience sophistication is precisely what the member is supposed to consider in deciding what information to provide. Fairness of presentation does not mean uniformity of detail: an unsophisticated retail audience and an institutional client can properly receive different levels of detail, provided what each receives is fair, accurate, and complete.
rationales.C: Identical boilerplate is the opposite of what the guidance calls for. The recommended practice is to consider the knowledge and sophistication of the audience to whom the presentation is addressed and to tailor the information accordingly, alongside composite presentation, inclusion of terminated accounts, disclosures that fully explain the results, and retention of the supporting data and records.

questions.stem: When a performance presentation is brief, Standard III(D) most likely requires the detailed supporting information to be:

options.A: Made available to clients and prospects on request.
options.B: Not required in any form.
options.C: Sent unsolicited to every recipient.

rationales.A: If the presentation is brief, the member or candidate must make available to clients and prospects, on request, the detailed information supporting that communication. Best practice dictates that brief presentations include a reference to the limited nature of the information provided, so that the recipient knows there is further detail to ask for.
rationales.B: A brief presentation does not extinguish the obligation. The detailed information supporting the communication must be made available to clients and prospects on request, and best practice is for the brief presentation itself to note the limited nature of what it contains.
rationales.C: The obligation is availability on request, not unsolicited distribution. The member must be able to supply the supporting detail when a client or prospect asks for it; nothing in Standard III(D) requires that the detail be pushed out to everyone who received the brief presentation.

questions.stem: Paper was one of five managers of an equity fund. With his firm's written permission, he presents the fund's entire performance history to prospective clients to demonstrate his own past success. Paper most likely:

options.A: violated the Code and Standards by claiming the fund's record as his own.
options.B: violated the Code and Standards by including prior employer results.
options.C: did not violate the Code and Standards.

rationales.A: Paper violated the Code and Standards by claiming the performance of the entire fund as his own. Even though the firm granted written permission, the performance is that of a team of five managers, not Paper alone, and presenting it as his personal track record without clarifying his contribution is misleading. Standard III(D) requires that performance be fair, accurate, and complete, and attributing team results to an individual misrepresents that individual's role.
rationales.B: Showing results earned at a prior employer is not itself the violation: past performance of accounts managed at a prior firm may be shown as part of a track record so long as it is accompanied by appropriate disclosure of where the performance took place and the person's specific role in achieving it. Paper's failure is one of attribution rather than of venue, because the record belongs to a team of five and he presents it as his own.
rationales.C: Team performance is not personal performance. Even with the firm's written permission, the history was produced by five managers, so presenting the entire fund's record as a demonstration of Paper's own past success is misleading and breaches Standard III(D)'s requirement that performance presentation be fair, accurate, and complete.

questions.stem: Under Standard III(D), showing the past performance of accounts managed at a prior firm as part of a track record is most likely:

options.A: Prohibited in all circumstances.
options.B: Permitted without qualification or disclosure.
options.C: Permitted with disclosure of where it occurred and the member's role.

rationales.A: There is no categorical prohibition. Prior-firm history may be shown as part of a performance track record when it is accompanied by appropriate disclosures about where the performance took place and the person's specific role in achieving it. The concern of Standard III(D) is misattribution, not the identity of the former employer.
rationales.B: Unqualified presentation misattributes the record. Disclosure is the condition on which prior-firm performance may be shown: the member must state where the performance was earned and what his or her specific role in achieving it was, so that a prospective client is not left to assume the record was produced single-handedly at the member's current firm.
rationales.C: Standard III(D) does not prohibit showing past performance of accounts managed at a prior firm as part of a performance track record, as long as showing that record is accompanied by appropriate disclosures about where the performance took place and the person's specific role in achieving that performance. Those disclosures are what keep the presentation fair, accurate, and complete.

questions.stem: Under Standard III(E), information received from a client is most appropriately disclosed to:

options.A: Authorized fellow employees who also work for that client.
options.B: No one, in any circumstances.
options.C: Any colleague at the firm.

rationales.A: Members and candidates should avoid disclosing any information received from a client except to authorized fellow employees who are also working for that client. They must understand and follow their firm's electronic information communication and storage procedures; if the firm does not have procedures in place, they should encourage the development of procedures that appropriately reflect the firm's size and business operations. They should also encourage their firm to conduct regular periodic training on confidentiality procedures for all firm personnel, including noninvestment staff who have routine direct contact with clients and their records.
rationales.B: Confidentiality is not absolute secrecy. Authorized colleagues who are also working for the client are the recognized exception, since serving the client often requires that information be shared within the service team; disclosure may also be required where the law compels it or where the information concerns illegal activities.
rationales.C: Sharing is limited to authorized fellow employees who are also working for that client, not extended to the firm at large. Owing the same professional duties does not give every colleague a need to know, which is why firms maintain electronic communication and storage procedures and periodic confidentiality training for all personnel.

questions.stem: For a client who may become vulnerable, a secondary contact is most appropriately established:

options.A: Only once signs of diminished capacity appear.
options.B: Never, as it intrudes on client privacy.
options.C: At the beginning of the client relationship.

rationales.A: Waiting for warning signs defeats the purpose. Best practice is to establish the secondary contact at the beginning of the client relationship, before any need arises, because a client whose capacity has already diminished may no longer be able to nominate a trusted person or to give permission for that person to be contacted.
rationales.B: A client-designated contact is a protective best practice, not a privacy intrusion: the client chooses the person and permits the contact in advance, so nothing is disclosed without the client's own authorization. The nominated contact provides an avenue to prevent and address potential financial abuse of the client.
rationales.C: Best practice for members and candidates is to establish a secondary contact at the beginning of the client relationship. That contact could be a trusted family member, a legal adviser, or some other third-party intermediary whom the client permits contacting should concerns arise about the client's ability to make informed decisions about his or her finances. The nominated secondary contact provides members and candidates an avenue to prevent and/or address potential financial abuse of the client.

questions.stem: To protect the interests of a vulnerable investor, a member is most likely expected to:

options.A: Defer entirely to the client's legal guardian.
options.B: Set aside firm policies on vulnerable clients case by case.
options.C: Comply with the firm's policies on vulnerable clients.

rationales.A: The member takes affirmative protective steps rather than treating the matter as someone else's. Those steps begin with complying with firm policies and procedures dealing with vulnerable clients and extend to asking for a secondary contact when every account is opened, training to understand the issues and to interact with clients who may exhibit diminished mental capacity, following internal reporting procedures when concerns are raised, and additional compliance review of such accounts.
rationales.B: Complying with the firm's policies and procedures for vulnerable clients is the listed step, not optional guidance to be applied at the member's discretion. Those policies exist precisely so that the response to a vulnerable client does not depend on an individual's case-by-case judgment, and internal reporting procedures must be followed when concerns are raised.
rationales.C: Members and candidates should take steps to protect the interests of vulnerable investors by complying with any firm policies and procedures specifically dealing with vulnerable clients, asking for a secondary contact during the establishment of every account, undertaking training and education to understand issues related to vulnerable investors, undergoing training on how to interact and address issues with clients who may exhibit diminished mental capacity, following internal firm reporting procedures when concerns are raised, and implementing additional compliance review for the accounts of vulnerable investors.

questions.stem: With respect to electronically stored client information, Standard III(E) most likely requires a member to:

options.A: Become an expert in information security technology.
options.B: Treat electronic storage as free of disclosure risk.
options.C: Be particularly aware of potential accidental disclosures.

rationales.A: Standard III(E) does not require members or candidates to become experts in information security technology. What it expects is heightened awareness of the risk of accidental disclosure and a thorough understanding of the employer's policies for ensuring the security of confidential information maintained by the firm.
rationales.B: Electronic storage increases accidental-disclosure exposure rather than removing it, and that is the reason for the guidance. Many employers have strict policies about how to electronically communicate sensitive client information and about storing client information on personal laptops, mobile devices, or external storage devices or systems.
rationales.C: Because of the ever-increasing use of electronically stored information, members and candidates need to be particularly aware of potential accidental disclosures. Many employers have strict policies about how to electronically communicate sensitive client information and store client information on personal laptops, mobile devices, or external storage devices or systems. Standard III(E) does not require members or candidates to become experts in information security technology, but they should have a thorough understanding of the policies of their employer for ensuring the security of confidential information maintained by the firm.

questions.stem: With respect to an investigation by Professional Conduct at CFA Institute, Standard III(E) most likely:

options.A: Conditions cooperation on written client consent.
options.B: Permits cooperation with the investigation.
options.C: Requires refusal of requests involving client matters.

rationales.A: No client-consent precondition attaches to cooperation with a Professional Conduct investigation. Members and candidates must cooperate with investigations into their own conduct unless prevented from doing so by law, and Professional Conduct will exercise reasonable care to ensure that all documents and information it receives during an investigation remain confidential.
rationales.B: Standard III(E) does not prevent members and candidates from cooperating with an investigation by Professional Conduct at CFA Institute. Instead, members and candidates must cooperate with investigations into their conduct unless prevented from doing so by law. Under the CFA Institute Rules of Procedure for Conduct Related to the Profession, as amended and restated 1 January 2022, members and candidates are also required to cooperate with investigations into the conduct of others. Professional Conduct will exercise reasonable care to ensure that all documents and information it receives during an investigation remain confidential.
rationales.C: Standard III(E) does not prevent cooperation with a Professional Conduct investigation, so refusal is not what the standard calls for. Cooperation is in fact mandatory, with respect to investigations into the member's own conduct and into the conduct of others, unless the law prevents it; confidentiality of the material supplied is protected by Professional Conduct itself.
